newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow blames U.S. for missile talks stalemate.
newsitem.headline: Moscow blames U.S. for missile talks stalemate.

text.p: Russia blamed the United States on Saturday for the failure of talks in Geneva on regional missile defences, saying Washington's representative was too junior to allow the negotiations to succeed.

In a statement reflecting mutual irritation between Moscow and Washington over the issue, the Russian foreign ministry said the documents were not signed "because the American side in Geneva was not represented at the agreed level" and the U.S. negotiator lacked authority to resolve outstanding issues.
Russia was represented at the talks by Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Mamedov, while the U.S. sent a lower-level diplomat, Stanley Riveles, instead of Undersecretary of State Lynn Davis.

The Russian statement, reported by Interfax news agency, accused the United States of "dropping the barrier" on the talks in advance by announcing in Washington earlier this week that the agreement would not be signed.
"The talks had not yet started and a State Department representative had already pronounced the death sentence on them," the Russian statement said, clearly referring to spokesman Nicholas Burns.

The statement said the two sides had "serious differences" over the second stage of the agreement setting out guidelines for regional missile defences and it accused the U.S. side of showing no enthusiasm for this part of the deal.
The U.S. was refusing to give guarantees that the anti-missile systems under discussion in the first stage would not be deployed while the talks were still in progress, the Russian statement said.

It called on Washington to show "political will" to complete work on the first stage agreement. Washington has blamed Russia for backing out of the October 31 signing, saying Moscow wanted to tie it to further progress on the second stage.

Russia is adamant that regional missile defence systems should not undermine the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (ABM). The two countries announced in September that work was complete on a first stage deal covering slower missile systems, leaving faster systems to be negotiated later.
